description: We are human beings from for_code (Computing Academic League of the School of Chemistry at Federal University of Rio de Janeiro). We want to use our skills to solve real world problems.
summary:
Understanding how precipitation patterns change over time is essential for identifying environmental trends and supporting regional planning. However, these changes do not occur uniformly: different regions may experience increasing rainfall, decreasing rainfall, or more frequent periods of unusually dry or wet conditions.

To address this challenge, we developed for_ecast, an interactive climate analytics platform focused on precipitation patterns across all Brazilian states and the Federal District. The platform transforms historical rainfall records into accessible visualizations, allowing users to explore monthly variations, identify anomalies, and investigate long-term trends in different regions.

Beyond visualization, for_ecast combines statistical analysis and machine learning. It uses the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope estimator to investigate the direction, magnitude, and statistical significance of precipitation trends. It also implements a Random Forest model to generate short-term rainfall forecasts, which can be compared against a seasonal baseline.

By bringing historical analysis, statistical validation, and predictive modeling together, for_ecast helps users understand not only how precipitation has changed, but also how its historical patterns can inform future estimates.
details:
The methodological foundation of for_ecast is inspired by NASA's scientific study, "Time-Series Analysis of Remotely-Sensed SeaWiFS Chlorophyll in River-Influenced Coastal Regions" (2009). Building on its approach to environmental time-series analysis, our project adapts these concepts to investigate a different variable: precipitation. Instead of analyzing chlorophyll concentrations in coastal regions, for_ecast applies time-series analysis to rainfall data across Brazilian states, identifying anomalies and historical trends. We further extend this approach through statistical significance testing and machine learning-based forecasts.

for_ecast collects daily accumulated precipitation data through the Meteomatics Weather API, using spatial polygon queries corresponding to Brazilian state boundaries. The collected records are processed into monthly and annual time series, providing a historical overview of precipitation patterns across the country.

The system operates through dual analytical engines:

Statistical Analysis: The statistical engine investigates precipitation variability, seasonality, monthly anomalies, and annual trends across Brazilian states.

Daily precipitation records are aggregated into monthly and annual totals. Incomplete periods are excluded from analyses requiring complete observations to ensure consistent comparisons.

To classify monthly precipitation anomalies, each month is compared with the historical records of the same calendar month at the corresponding location. Historical P10, P30, P70, and P90 percentiles define five categories: very dry, dry, normal, wet, and very wet. Deviations from historical averages are also expressed in millimeters, percentages, and standardized Z-scores.

For annual trend detection, for_ecast combines the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test with Sen's slope estimator. This allows users to identify whether precipitation is increasing or decreasing, estimate the magnitude of these changes in millimeters per year, and evaluate their statistical significance.

The analysis also considers temporal autocorrelation through the Ljung-Box test and applies the Hamed-Rao variance correction when required. Benjamini-Hochberg and Holm adjustments are available to account for multiple statistical comparisons across reference locations, with an adjusted p-value below 0.05 used as the significance threshold.

Machine Learning: The predictive engine uses a Random Forest Regressor trained on historical precipitation data from 2006 to 2025. The model incorporates temporal features, including cyclical month encoding using sine and cosine transformations, historical precipitation lags (1, 2, 3, and 12 months), and rolling averages over 3 and 12 months.

These features are constructed using historical observations to preserve temporal separation during model evaluation. The system generates monthly precipitation forecasts and supports recursive multi-step projections over an experimental horizon of up to 12 months.

To evaluate predictive performance, the Random Forest model is compared against a Seasonal Baseline, which serves as a reference based on historical seasonal patterns. Users can examine state-specific Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) to understand how the models perform and whether machine learning provides an advantage over the simpler seasonal approach.

for_ecast: Data for Tomorrow

for_ecast makes historical precipitation analysis more accessible by transforming complex environmental data into regional insights. Students, researchers, and other interested users can explore rainfall patterns, identify statistically significant trends, recognize unusually dry or wet periods, and compare predictive models.

By combining historical observations, statistical methods, and experimental forecasts, the platform provides an interactive way to investigate how precipitation patterns vary across Brazil and how these changes can inform regional environmental planning and adaptation.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The project was developed using a combination of Python for data processing, statistical analysis, and machine learning, and web technologies for the interactive dashboard.

  • Programming languages: Python 3, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3. SVG was also used for charts and editable visual elements.
  • Python libraries and tools: Pandas and NumPy, data cleaning, manipulation, and numerical calculations; SciPy, statistical analysis and tests; Matplotlib, data visualization and statistical charts; Scikit-learn, machine learning models, including Random Forest and model evaluation; Requests, API data collection; Pytest, automated testing.
  • Data sources and APIs: The project includes precipitation data collected through the Meteomatics API, along with historical datasets organized in CSV files.
  • Software and development tools: Git for version control, Python's built-in HTTP server for running the dashboard locally, and a web browser to access and interact with the dashboard. Figma is included in the dashboard documentation as a design and implementation reference.
  • Dashboard technologies: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and inline SVG. The dashboard uses locally generated JSON data and does not require a hosted database, external browser APIs, or third-party JavaScript frameworks.
  • Hardware: The project was developed as a software-based workflow on a standard computer. No specialized hardware, such as GPUs, servers, or dedicated scientific equipment, is documented as a requirement.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI):

  • Claude IA: Assisted in data preparation, descriptive statistics, definition of precipitation categories, monthly anomaly analysis, trend analysis, and historical time-series comparisons.
  • ChatGPT: Utilized to adapt integration code for correct data ingestion, implement dashboard features, and handle methodological refinements—such as documenting full vs. expanding percentile classification modes, adjusting decadal comparative test interpretations for unequal sample sizes, preserving reference point identifiers alongside state codes (UF), and documenting dashboard architecture.
  • GitHub Copilot: Used for real-time code completion, syntax optimization, and resolving command and scripting issues within the interactive dashboard scripts.
